---
title: "Reproducing the analysis of Domínguez-García et al. (2019)"
author: "Simon Frost"
engine: julia
---

## Overview

Domínguez-García, Dakos and Kéfi (2019, *PNAS* 116:25714) computed 27 stability metrics for
thousands of simulated food webs and asked how they are related. Their answer was three
groups of correlated metrics, which they called *early response to pulse*, *sensitivities to
press* and *distance to threshold*. This vignette repeats their statistical analysis on their
own data (Dataset S2, 100 communities for each richness from 5 to 99 species). Each step is
also checked against the output of their Python code. The next vignettes regenerate the data
themselves.

```{julia}
using EcologicalResilience
using DataFrames, Statistics, Random, Printf
using LinearAlgebra: I
using Plots
data = joinpath(pkgdir(EcologicalResilience), "data", "dominguez-garcia2019")
df = read_metrics(joinpath(data, "Dataset_S2.csv"))
size(df)
```

`read_metrics` reads the raw columns of the authors' GitHub deposit. It then applies the
transformations of their `prepare_dataframe`, so that a larger value of each metric means a
more stable community. The result equals the publisher's version of Dataset S2 to within
4e-13.

## Correlations change with community size

For each richness, `size_correlations` computes the 27 × 27 Spearman correlation matrix (and
two covariance matrices used later).

```{julia}
sc = size_correlations(df)
li = Dict(l => i for (i, l) in enumerate(sc.labels))
ρ(a, b) = sc.rho[li[a], li[b], :]
trailing(x, k = 6) = [i < k ? NaN : mean(x[(i - k + 1):i]) for i in eachindex(x)]
pairs = [("TM", "<TM>"), ("Is", "tmax"), ("Rinf", "<s_ij>"), ("RM", "SM")]
plot([plot(sc.sizes, ρ(a, b); label = "per size", alpha = 0.4, title = "$a vs $b", ylim = (-1, 1)) for (a, b) in pairs]...;
     layout = (2, 2), size = (800, 550), xlabel = "species richness", ylabel = "Spearman ρ")
for (k, (a, b)) in enumerate(pairs)
    plot!(sc.sizes, trailing(ρ(a, b)); subplot = k, label = "rolling mean of 6", lw = 2)
end
current()
```

These are the four pairs of the paper's Figure 1. Like the authors' code, the smoothed curve is
a *trailing* mean of six sizes, although SI §1 says it is centred.

SI §1 classifies each of the 351 pairs by how its correlation differs between small (5–15),
medium and large (85–95) communities. The authors' code uses some windows that differ
slightly from the text (5–14 for one test, and 50–59 for "medium").

```{julia}
types = correlation_types(sc)
combine(groupby(types, :type), nrow => :pairs)
```

These are the counts the authors' code produces: 155 pairs (44%) are unchanged (G), and most of
the others weaken (F, 105) or strengthen (E, 64) between small and medium communities, then
stay constant.

## Networks of metrics and their groups

For each size class, the correlations are averaged over the sizes in the class. A network is
then built with the metrics as nodes and the absolute mean correlations as edge weights.
Modularity measures how well a partition separates strongly connected groups.

```{julia}
groups_of(g) = [sc.labels[g .== k] for k in 1:maximum(g)]
results = map(SIZE_CLASSES) do (name, (lo, hi))
    R, _ = class_average(sc, lo, hi)
    W = metric_network(R)
    g, Q = modular_groups(W; runs = 50, rng = Xoshiro(1))
    name => (R = R, W = W, groups = g, Q = Q)
end |> Dict
for name in ("small", "medium", "large")
    r = results[name]
    @printf("%-6s Q = %.4f\n", name, r.Q)
    foreach(m -> println("   ", join(m, " ")), groups_of(r.groups))
end
```

The paper reports a best partition with modularity Q = 0.177 from ten Gephi runs. The Louvain
method here finds Q = 0.1767 on the medium class, so the paper's figure most likely refers to
that class. The partition shipped with the authors' code, which is the same file for all three
classes, scores a little lower:

```{julia}
shipped = Dict("MAmax" => 0, "Mtmax" => 0, "MR0" => 0, "Amax" => 1, "R0" => 1, "tmax" => 1,
               "RM" => 3, "<RM>" => 3, "<SE>" => 3, "maxSE" => 3, "SM" => 3, "<SM>" => 3, "maxRE" => 3,
               "maxSM" => 3, "maxRM" => 3, "<RE>" => 3)
gship = [get(shipped, l, 2) for l in sc.labels]
[@sprintf("%s: Q(shipped) = %.4f, Q(Louvain) = %.4f", n, modularity(results[n].W, gship), results[n].Q)
 for n in ("small", "medium", "large")]
```

The three groups of the paper are clear in every class: the median pulse metrics (MR0, MAmax,
Mtmax); the resistance and sensitivity of biomass to presses and extinctions; and resilience,
invariability, sensitivity and tolerance. The metrics the paper calls idiosyncratic (R0, Amax,
tmax) move between groups as the communities grow.

## Hierarchical clustering

The paper describes average-linkage clustering on the distance d = 1 − ρ. The authors' code
instead clusters the rows of |ρ| as profiles, using correlation distance. `metric_dendrogram`
does either.

```{julia}
R = results["medium"].R
dd = metric_dendrogram(R)
order = dd.tree.order
heatmap(sc.labels[order], sc.labels[order], R[order, order]; c = :RdBu, clim = (-1, 1),
        xrotation = 90, size = (700, 620), title = "Medium communities, ordered by the dendrogram")
```

```{julia}
for (name, (lo, hi)) in SIZE_CLASSES
    R, _ = class_average(sc, lo, hi)
    a, b = metric_dendrogram(R), metric_dendrogram(R; distance = :one_minus_rho)
    @printf("%-6s as coded: %.3f (vs its own distance %.3f); with d = 1 − ρ: %.3f\n", name, a.c_code, a.c_clustering,
            b.c_clustering)
end
```

The coefficient the authors print (as coded) compares the tree with a Euclidean distance it was
not built from. Its medium-class value, 0.846, is the c = 0.85 of the paper.

## How much variance can a few metrics capture?

For each metric, `explained_variance` gives the share of the total variance of the
(mean/range-normalised) metrics that it accounts for through its covariances (SI §6).

```{julia}
Σ, _ = class_average(sc, 45, 55; field = :valuecov)
ev, own = explained_variance(Σ)
sort(DataFrame(metric = sc.labels, explained = ev, own = own), :explained; rev = true)[1:8, :]
```

These values equal the Python output to 1e-16. The paper's comparison of three metrics taken
from one group with three taken from different groups uses the volume of the rank-covariance
ellipsoid (SI §7). The volume is scaled so that independent metrics of equal variance give 1.

```{julia}
Σr, _ = class_average(sc, 45, 55; field = :rankcov)
g = results["medium"].groups
vol(ms) = ellipsoid_volume(Σr[ms, ms]) / ellipsoid_volume(Matrix(1.0I, 3, 3))
rng = Xoshiro(1234)
big = [findall(==(k), g) for k in 1:maximum(g) if count(==(k), g) > 3]
within = [mean(vol(randperm(rng, length(G))[1:3] |> p -> G[p]) for _ in 1:2000) for G in big]
across = mean(vol([rand(rng, G) for G in big]) for _ in 1:2000)
(within_groups = round.(within; digits = 3), one_per_group = round(across; digits = 3))
```

With three large groups in the medium class, three metrics from different groups span more of the space than three from one group. This is
the paper's argument for measuring one metric from each group.
